implementation_notes: Kotlin supports delegation natively: the `by` clause in the supertype list stores the delegate inside the object and the compiler generates every interface member forwarding to it, so the abstract base decorator of the classic structure simply vanishes and a decorator overrides only the members whose behaviour changes. The language reference describes this as zero-boilerplate delegation, and it is the default way to wrap a repository, sender or service interface. Two limits keep the classic form relevant: `by` works only for interfaces (a concrete class cannot be decorated this way), and members overridden in the decorator are not visible to the delegate, which keeps using its own implementations - so self-referential behaviour has to be handled explicitly.
idiom_name: interface delegation with `by`: class Wrapper(delegate: Repo) : Repo by delegate
pitfalls: Members you override are not called by the delegate: a generated member that internally calls another interface member reaches the delegate's own implementation, not your override.

Delegation is interface-only - wrapping a concrete class requires hand-written forwarding or an adapter - and delegating to a nullable or reassignable delegate expression fails in ways the compiler does not always explain clearly.

When two delegated interfaces declare the same member the class must override it explicitly (and decide which delegate wins); relying on the compiler to resolve the clash silently is impossible, but a wrong explicit override is easy to write.
